parakeet: That's the real challenge here, because secular morality is often accused of moving too much. But biblical morality only appears stable if you never look closely at how people actually use it. In real life, believers are not following every command, every punishment, every purity code, every hierarchy, every divine judgment the same way. They are already selecting, already filtering, already deciding what really applies and what was for that time. That means the actual moral work is already being done by human beings, not by the text alone. So the question is not whether morality shifts, of course it does. The real question is what it shifts toward. Does it shift toward greater empathy, greater freedom, greater justice, greater consistency in the protection of human well-being, or does it shift only when believers are forced to drag ancient law into moral relevance through modern values they pretend did not come from modernity? A moral code does not become timeless just because people call it timeless. A moral code deserves to be called timeless only if it can survive ethical examination across time. If it can still make moral sense when human understanding deepens, if it can still be defended when we know more about trauma, power, human development, coercion, psychology, and social harm than ancient writers ever did. That is where scripture begins to crack. Because many divine commands do not fail modern ethics merely because modern people are too soft. They fail because they ignore or override obvious human harm. They place obedience above well being, authority above consequence, loyalty above compassion. And once the moral system starts excusing suffering simply because it came from above, it stops being morally serious and starts becoming morally dangerous. Modern ethics, at their best, do not ask us to bow before an ancient command and then explain away the blood on the floor. They ask us to face the consequences of our values honestly. They ask whether a rule reduces suffering or multiplies it, whether it protects dignity or crushes it, whether it creates conditions for flourishing or simply secures obedience. That is a much stronger philosophical basis for morality than God said so, especially when what God supposedly said so often reflects the assumptions of ancient tribal life rather than universal human care.
